The manipulation of time in the story is masterfully balanced and serves the emotional core of the narrative. The first four sections of the story stretch out a single Saturday visit, moving slowly through the hours (ten o'clock, eleven, one, three, five, and dusk). This deliberate, unhurried pacing mirrors the quiet, repetitive rhythms of the aging mother's life and allows the reader to absorb the subtle details of her stubbornness, frailty, and deep affection for the narrator. 

In the final section, the author abruptly compresses a month of story time—covering a medical emergency, a hospital stay, and two weeks of recovery at a cousin's house—into just two short paragraphs. This sudden acceleration effectively conveys the jarring nature of the crisis and prevents the story from becoming a melodrama about hospitalization. When the narrator returns to the house, the pacing slows back down to real-time, allowing the reader to feel the lingering impact of the time that has passed (seen in the rotting garden) before settling back into the comforting, familiar rhythm of the characters' relationship.
